almanacforager:codex-habitat.flyagaric: Birch and pine, autumn forest floor
almanacforager:codex-habitat.blueberry: Acid soils, heath and pine woods
almanacforager:codex-description.basil: Aromatic annual of the mint family. The leaves bruise easily and lose their oil within a day; best picked just before use.
almanacforager:codex-description.chamomi: Daisy-like annual with apple-scented flowers. Long taken as a calming infusion before sleep.
almanacforager:codex-description.cilantr: Pungent annual; the green leaf and the dry seed (coriander) carry quite different flavours from the same plant.
almanacforager:codex-description.lavende: Woody perennial; the dried flower keeps its scent for years and was burned to sweeten linens.
almanacforager:codex-description.marjora: Sweet-scented oregano relative. Tender; does not survive hard frost.
almanacforager:codex-description.mint: Aromatic perennial. Spreads by rhizome and is hard to be rid of once rooted; the leaves keep their oil best when dried slowly out of sunlight.
almanacforager:codex-description.saffron: The dried red stigmas of an autumn-flowering crocus. Three threads to a flower; an ounce demands many thousand blossoms.
almanacforager:codex-description.sage: Grey-green woody perennial long burned for purification and steeped in cold water against fevers.
almanacforager:codex-description.thyme: Low woody groundcover. The oil resists spoilage and was rubbed into hung meat.
almanacforager:codex-description.almondm: Garden agaric with a faint almond scent. Cultivated on warm compost in sheds and stables.
almanacforager:codex-description.bearded: Pendant white teeth in a frozen waterfall on broken hardwood. Long in the medicine of the eastern apothecaries.
almanacforager:codex-description.bitterb: Looks much like a king bolete; the bitterness reveals itself only on the tongue and ruins any pot it joins.
almanacforager:codex-description.blacktr: A black hollow funnel that vanishes into leaf shadow. Dries to a fragrant smoky powder.
almanacforager:codex-description.bluemea: A small dung-loving agaric that bruises blue at the slightest pressure. The bruising marks the active alkaloid.
almanacforager:codex-description.chanter: Yellow trumpet with false gills, smelling faintly of apricot. Forms a fungal ring with oak and beech.
almanacforager:codex-description.chicken: Sulphur-orange shelves on living oak. Tender at the growing edge; woody and inedible deep within.
almanacforager:codex-description.commonm: Honeycomb cap on a hollow stem. Often follows fire by a single season and rarely a second.
almanacforager:codex-description.deathca: An olive-green cap with a sheathed base. Mistaken for the field mushroom by the careless; the toxin destroys the liver days after the meal.
almanacforager:codex-description.deerear: Asymmetric ochre cup, split down one side. Ascomycete; not a true gilled mushroom.
almanacforager:codex-description.devilbo: Pale-capped bolete with a blood-red stem and pores. The flesh blues sharply at the cut.
almanacforager:codex-description.devilst: Bleeds a thick red liquid from its young teeth. The liquid bears a known anticoagulant.
almanacforager:codex-description.dryadsa: A scaly bracket on standing dead wood, smelling of cucumber when fresh. Tough but edible while young.
almanacforager:codex-description.earthba: A leathery yellow ball that splits and puffs black spores. Looks like a puffball; is not, and is poisonous.
almanacforager:codex-description.elfinsa: White lobed saddle on a fluted stem. Contains a heat-labile toxin; long boiling renders it edible.
almanacforager:codex-description.fieldmu: Pasture agaric, brown gills turning black with age. The most-eaten wild mushroom of the temperate world.
almanacforager:codex-description.flyagar: Red cap freckled with white veil. Long associated with the birch; long associated with northern shamanic practice.
almanacforager:codex-description.foolsco: Small slender lawn agaric. Carries the same toxin as the death cap and is often mistaken for harmless inkcaps.
almanacforager:codex-description.funeral: Tan agaric on rotting conifer wood. Looks much like a winter wine cap and shares the deadly amatoxin family.
almanacforager:codex-description.goldcap: Tropical dung-loving agaric, golden crown bruising blue. Long known to the cultivators of cattle ground.
almanacforager:codex-description.golddro: Bleeds a golden milk that yellows further on contact with air. Acrid; eaten only after long curing.
almanacforager:codex-description.greencr: Cap cracked into a green mosaic. One of the few russulas that is mild rather than peppery.
almanacforager:codex-description.honeymu: Bundled honey-coloured caps on stumps and roots. The mycelium glows faintly at night and may be the largest organism on earth.
almanacforager:codex-description.indigom: Cap and gills indigo blue; the milk runs the same colour. Eaten in the pine country of the new world.
almanacforager:codex-description.jackola: Bright orange clusters on oak roots, glowing faintly in the dark. Toxic; mistaken often for the chanterelle.
almanacforager:codex-description.kingbol: Stout brown cap and white pores. The most prized of the boletes; dried, it carries deep through winter.
almanacforager:codex-description.laughin: Bright orange cluster on hardwood, bitter at every age. Bears mild psychoactive alkaloids and the bitterness deters most foragers.
almanacforager:codex-description.liberty: Slender brown agaric with a pointed cap. Bruises blue and bears psilocybin in measurable quantity.
almanacforager:codex-description.livermu: Crimson tongue on old oak, bleeding red juice when cut. Acidic, with an iron taste.
almanacforager:codex-description.lobster: Not a single mushroom but a parasitic mould (Hypomyces) that has overgrown a milkcap and turned it orange.
almanacforager:codex-description.orangeo: Stout bolete with a brick-orange cap. The flesh blackens when cut; cooks dark.
almanacforager:codex-description.paddyst: Tropical agaric grown for centuries on rice straw. Eaten young, before the cap opens.
almanacforager:codex-description.pinkbon: Small pink-capped agaric, fragrant of radish. Common but easily missed in fallen beech leaves.
almanacforager:codex-description.pinkoys: Hot-climate oyster relative; cap and gills the colour of salmon flesh.
almanacforager:codex-description.puffbal: A spherical fruiting body that ripens to dust. The young flesh is white and edible; the mature spores were once dropped on bleeding wounds.
almanacforager:codex-description.redwine: Burgundy-capped agaric of garden mulch beds. Cultivated in wood chips; spreads aggressively and feeds the soil.
almanacforager:codex-description.reishi: Bracket fungus of dead hardwood. Slow-growing; the specimen records years. Long-prized in eastern medicine for its bitter polysaccharides.
almanacforager:codex-description.saffron: Carrot-orange cap and gills, bleeding orange milk. The flesh greens with handling.
almanacforager:codex-description.shiitak: Cultivated for at least a thousand years on hardwood logs. Smoky and savoury when dried.
almanacforager:codex-description.sickene: Bright red cap on white stem. Acrid raw, and earns its name; long boiling renders it tolerable but rarely worth the trouble.
almanacforager:codex-description.tinderh: Hard hoof-shaped bracket on birch. The inner felt has carried a smouldering ember between camps for ten thousand years.
almanacforager:codex-description.violetw: Deep violet from cap to stem. The cobwebbed veil is the diagnostic of the wider Cortinarius genus.
almanacforager:codex-description.wavycap: Wavy-margined brown cap on wood-chip beds. Bruises blue and bears the same alkaloids as the liberty cap.
almanacforager:codex-description.whiteoy: Cream-coloured shelf clusters on dead hardwood. Cold-tolerant; fruits well into winter.
almanacforager:codex-description.witchha: Conical waxcap that blackens with age and handling. Marks unfertilised old grassland.
almanacforager:codex-description.bluebel: Drooping blue bells on a single stem. A carpet of these marks ancient woodland and is taken slow to form.
almanacforager:codex-description.catmint: Grey-leaved perennial of the mint family. Cats are drawn to the bruised leaf; the dry herb steeps as a calming tea.
almanacforager:codex-description.cornflo: Slim blue flower of cereal field margins. Once common in rye and now scarce where the field is sprayed clean.
almanacforager:codex-description.cowpars: Tall lacy white umbel, the first of the summer hedgerow. The hollow stems were once cut for whistles.
almanacforager:codex-description.daffodi: Trumpet-flower of damp pasture, lifting in the first warmth of spring. All parts toxic if eaten.
almanacforager:codex-description.edelwei: White wool-felted star of high alpine rock. Long the proof a man had climbed.
almanacforager:codex-description.forgetm: Five-petalled blue flower with a yellow eye. Holds its bloom into late summer in damp ground.
almanacforager:codex-description.ghostpi: A leafless white plant of deep shade. Bears no chlorophyll; draws its sustenance from forest fungi by way of nearby tree roots.
almanacforager:codex-description.goldenp: Bright orange-yellow poppy of dry slopes. Shuts at evening and in cloud.
almanacforager:codex-description.heather: Low woody shrub of acid moorland. Honey gathered from heather flowers carries a thick, dark character.
almanacforager:codex-description.horseta: Jointed segmented stems with no true flower. An ancient lineage; the stems carry silica enough to scour pewter.
almanacforager:codex-description.lilyoft: White paired bells on an arching stem, fragrant beyond their size. The whole plant is lethal to taste.
almanacforager:codex-description.mugwort: Tall grey-green perennial of waste ground. Long burned and bundled in northern medicine to mark threshold times.
almanacforager:codex-description.orangem: Orange five-petalled mallow of arid country. Roots run deep against drought.
almanacforager:codex-description.redtopg: Red-flowered meadow grass, the panicle airy as a haze in late summer.
almanacforager:codex-description.western: Yellow pea-flowered shrub, vicious with green spines and gold flowers at once.
almanacforager:codex-description.wilddai: White-rayed yellow-eyed daisy of close-cropped pasture. The flower closes by night and at the touch of rain.
almanacforager:codex-description.woad: Yellow-flowered biennial, leaves long fermented for a deep blue dye that preceded indigo in the old world.
almanacforager:codex-description.beautyb: Slender shrub bearing magenta drupes in tight whorls. Native to the warm broadleaf forests of the new world.
almanacforager:codex-description.blackbe: Thorned bramble of the hedgerow. Fruit ripens darkest at the tip of each cluster, where light reaches first.
almanacforager:codex-description.blackcu: Damp-ground shrub bearing strings of dark berries with a heavy musk. The bud is steeped for a clean infusion in the spring.
almanacforager:codex-description.blueber: Low acid-loving shrub. The blue bloom is a wax that rubs off; the fruit beneath is darker.
almanacforager:codex-description.cloudbe: Single golden berry on a low boreal-bog plant. Slow-ripening; rare south of the spruce line.
almanacforager:codex-description.cranber: Wiry mat of acid-bog ground. The red fruit floats; flooded harvest is the modern method.
almanacforager:codex-description.raspber: Caned bramble; the fruit slips from a white core when ripe. The leaf was steeped for women in the late stages of pregnancy.
almanacforager:codex-description.redcurr: Translucent red berries on a cool damp shrub. The juice sets to a stiff jelly without added pectin.
almanacforager:codex-description.strawbe: Low-growing herb with white flowers and red fruit. The fruit is botanically a cluster of seeds on a swollen receptacle, not a true berry.
almanacforager:codex-description.whitecu: Cultivar of the redcurrant lacking pigment. Sweeter than its red parent and much rarer.
almanacforager:codex-description.breadfr: Heavy starchy fruit of tropical lowlands. Roasted and pounded, it carries the body of a bread loaf.
almanacforager:codex-description.cherry: Stone fruit of a small spring-flowering tree. The wild form is bitter; cultivated cherries follow long selection.
almanacforager:codex-description.lychee: Pebbled red fruit with a pearly translucent flesh and a single seed. Subtropical; a season of three weeks.
almanacforager:codex-description.mango: Heavy resinous stone fruit of the tropics. Several thousand cultivars; little resemblance between hill and lowland fruit.
almanacforager:codex-description.orange: Round fragrant citrus of the warm latitudes. Hybrid in origin; carries the sour and sweet of both parents.
almanacforager:codex-description.peach: Velvet-skinned stone fruit of warm temperate orchards. Hybridises freely with apricot and almond.
almanacforager:codex-description.pear: Heavy gritty-fleshed pome. Improves in storage where apples decline; was set down in straw for winter eating.
almanacforager:codex-description.pinkapp: Pink-skinned apple cultivar of unknown origin in this country.
almanacforager:codex-description.pineapp: Spiny terrestrial bromeliad. The fruit is a fused mass; each diamond a single flower's remains.
almanacforager:codex-description.pomegra: Leather-skinned fruit packed with juice-jacketed seeds. Long-storing and long-symbolised.
almanacforager:codex-description.redappl: Red-skinned cultivated apple. The seed line of the apple does not run true; every apple from seed is a new thing.
almanacforager:codex-description.saguaro: Fruit of the giant Sonoran cactus, gathered from the arms with long poles cut from the same plant's ribs.
almanacforager:codex-description.yellowa: Yellow-skinned cultivated apple. Sweeter and softer than its red kin; bruises in transport.
almanacforager:codex-description.cabbage: Heavy leafy head of the brassica family. Late crop; the head sweetens after frost and was buried in pits for winter.
almanacforager:codex-description.carrot: Cultivated taproot. Wild ancestors are pale and bitter; the orange table carrot is a recent breeding.
almanacforager:codex-description.cassava: Heavy starchy tuber of the tropics. The raw flesh holds cyanide; long fermentation or grating-and-pressing renders it safe.
almanacforager:codex-description.cattail: Starchy rhizome of the marsh-edge cattail. Roasted and pounded for a coarse flour where wheat will not grow.
almanacforager:codex-description.papyrus: Thick starchy rhizome of the tropical papyrus. Eaten roasted in the dry season.
almanacforager:codex-description.fennel: Tall-stemmed perennial with a heavy aniseed scent. Bulb, leaf and seed were all kept separate in the herb garden.
almanacforager:codex-description.onion: Concentric-layered allium, sharp raw and sweet when cooked long. Stores for months in dry cool dark.
almanacforager:codex-description.parsnip: Pale taproot, related to the carrot; sweetened by the first hard frost. Older than the potato in northern cooking.
almanacforager:codex-description.pumpkin: Heavy fruit of a sprawling vine. Stored whole through the winter; the seed roasted for a separate food.
almanacforager:codex-description.turnip: Quick-growing brassica root. The tops are eaten as a green; the root keeps in clamps under straw.
almanacforager:codex-description.bellpep: Mild capsicum, the only fruit of the genus that is not pungent. Several colours from the same plant as the fruit ripens.
almanacforager:codex-description.amarant: Tall red-panicled grain of the warm new world. Both leaf and seed are eaten.
almanacforager:codex-description.flax: Slender blue-flowered annual. The seed yields oil; the stem yields the fibre that becomes linen after long retting.
almanacforager:codex-description.rice: Flooded-paddy cereal of the warm wet world. The most-grown grain by weight on the planet.
almanacforager:codex-description.rye: Cool-tolerant cereal that grows where wheat will not. Heavier loaf, darker crumb.
almanacforager:codex-description.spelt: Hulled ancestor of common wheat. The grain remains in its tough chaff after threshing and was milled in two stages.
almanacforager:codex-description.sunflow: Tall annual with a heavy head that tracks the sun before flowering. Seeds eaten whole or pressed for oil.
almanacforager:codex-description.peanut: A legume that buries its own pod after flowering. The seed ripens in the soil rather than the air.
almanacforager:codex-description.soybean: Cultivated legume of immense protein. Long fermented in the east as the base of many sauces and curds.
almanacforager:codex-description.licoric: Sweet-rooted perennial of dry steppe. The root is fifty times sweeter than cane sugar and was chewed for the throat.
almanacforager:codex-description.seagras: True flowering plant of the shallow coastal seabed. Not a seaweed; carries pollen on the current.
almanacforager:codex-description.seaweed: Cold-water alga of the tidal rocks. Dried and burned for soda and for iodine; eaten in many coastal cuisines.
almanacforager:codex-description.watercr: White-flowered aquatic buttercup. The leaves below water are thread-like; those above are flat.
almanacforager:codex-description.coopers: Tall perennial reed of marshes and brackish water. The hollow stems are split for thatch and for the flutework of barrels.
almanacforager:codex-description.papyrus: Tall sedge of slow tropical water. The pith was sliced, pressed and dried into the writing surface that bears its name.
almanacforager:codex-description.tule: Round-stemmed bulrush of freshwater marsh. Cut and bundled for canoes by the western peoples of the new world.
almanacforager:codex-description.brownse: Wet-meadow sedge with a drooping inflorescence. Leaves cut for fibre; rhizome holds river banks against scour.
almanacforager:codex-description.bamboo: Woody monocot. Hollow stem, no growth rings; the cane reaches its full height in a single season.
